::: notes
~1.5 min, and the scope-setting slide for the whole lecture. The nested rings are the standard containment view — AI contains machine learning, which contains neural networks and deep learning — but read them as a physicist: each ring is a broader hypothesis class. The point to make explicitly, because it is the common misconception: AI is much wider than deep learning. Symbolic AI, expert systems, and search dominated the field for decades; LLMs and agents are a current frontier we only touch in the futures section. What this lecture builds and demystifies, with runnable code, are the three starred methods — and crucially one of them, Bayesian optimisation with Gaussian processes, is classical probabilistic ML, not a neural network at all. So even our own three use cases span two rings, not one. Everything else on this map is real AI we are deliberately not covering today.
:::

## From neuron to Nobel Prize (1943–2024)

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import plotly.graph_objects as go

events = [
    (1943, "McCulloch-Pitts<br>neuron", 1, "#475569"),
    (1957, "Rosenblatt<br>Perceptron", -1, "#22d3ee"),
    (1969, "Minsky-Papert<br>(XOR limit)", 1, "#f87171"),
    (1982, "Hopfield<br>networks", -1, "#22d3ee"),
    (1986, "Backprop<br>(Rumelhart)", 1, "#22d3ee"),
    (1998, "LeNet<br>(LeCun)", -1, "#a78bfa"),
    (2006, "Deep belief<br>nets (Hinton)", 1, "#a78bfa"),
    (2012, "AlexNet<br>(ImageNet)", -1, "#fb923c"),
    (2017, "Transformers<br>(Attention)", 1, "#fb923c"),
    (2022, "ChatGPT", -1, "#f87171"),
    (2024, "Nobel Prize<br>Physics", 1, "#fbbf24"),
]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=1938, x1=2026, y0=0, y1=0,
    line=dict(color="#22d3ee", width=2.5))

for year, label, side, color in events:
    y_end = 0.52 * side
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=year, x1=year, y0=0, y1=y_end * 0.82,
        line=dict(color=color, width=1.5, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[year], y=[0], mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color=color, size=11, line=dict(color="#0d1b2a", width=2)),
        showlegend=False, hovertext=f"{year}: {label}"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=year, y=y_end,
        text=f"<b>{year}</b><br><span style='font-size:10px'>{label}</span>",
        showarrow=False, font=dict(size=11, color=color), align="center")

fig.update_layout(
    height=380, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#0d1b2a",
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10),
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False, range=[1936, 2027]),
    yaxis=dict(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False, range=[-0.9, 0.9]),
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"),
)
fig
```

::: notes
The yellow dot at 2024 is the Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Hopfield and Hinton — formally recognising that the foundations of modern AI are physics.

Note the two "winters" (after 1969 and after the late 1980s) — periods when funding and interest collapsed because the field overpromised. The current period since AlexNet in 2012 has been the longest sustained growth in AI history.
:::

## McCulloch & Pitts — the first artificial neuron (1943)

<div style="position:absolute; top:0.2em; right:0.4em; z-index:10;">
<img src="assets/Mccullochpitts.jpeg" style="width:165px; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4);">
</div>

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.2em;"}

::: {.column width="42%"}

**Warren McCulloch** & **Walter Pitts** — first mathematical model of a neuron, mapping neural firing onto Boolean logic (1943).

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.76em; margin:0.4em 0; line-height:1.6;"}
**How a neuron works:**

- **Dendrites** collect incoming signals from neighbouring neurons
- **Soma** integrates them as a weighted sum $\sum w_i x_i$
- Neuron **fires** if the sum exceeds threshold θ → signal propagates down the **axon**
:::

:::

::: {.column width="56%"}

<img src="assets/bio_neuron_annotated.png"
     style="height:auto; max-width:100%; max-height:31vh; border-radius:4px; display:block; margin:1.0em auto 0.2em auto;">

<img src="assets/mp_artificial_neuron.png"
     style="height:auto; max-width:100%; max-height:30vh; border-radius:4px; display:block; margin:0 auto;">

:::

::::

::: {.slide-ref}
McCulloch & Pitts (1943). A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity. *Bull. Math. Biophysics* 5, 115–133.
:::

::: notes
The starting point. McCulloch (a neurophysiologist) and Pitts (a logician) showed a neuron can be modelled as a threshold logic gate: take a weighted sum of inputs and fire if it exceeds a threshold θ. Two things to stress. First, the biological-to-mathematical mapping — dendrites are the inputs, the soma performs the weighted summation, the axon carries the output. Second, and crucially, the weights here are fixed by hand: there is no learning yet. Learning is what Rosenblatt adds on the next slide. So this is the architecture of a neuron without the ability to adapt.
:::

---

## The perceptron — first learning algorithm (1957)

::: {.col-left}

<img src="assets/portrait_rosenblatt.png" style="float:right; margin: 0 0 0.4em 0.8em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4); width:110px;">

**Frank Rosenblatt, 1957** — the Perceptron:

$$y = \text{sign}\!\left(\sum_i w_i x_i - \theta\right)$$

One neuron: $N$ weighted inputs $x_i$, one binary output $y$.
Unlike McCulloch-Pitts, the weights $w_i$ are **not fixed** — they are **learned** from labelled examples via an error-correction rule.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**The perceptron learning rule:**

$$w_i \leftarrow w_i + \eta \cdot (y - \hat{y}) \cdot x_i$$

Every modern network still follows this principle.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Rosenblatt's Mark 1 Perceptron (1958) was a physical hardware device — it made the front page of the New York Times.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Rosenblatt, F. (1958). The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. *Psychol. Rev.* 65(6), 386–408.
:::

::: notes
**Is the perceptron "a single neuron"?** Yes — exactly one neuron. The formula shows it: N inputs x_i each with a weight w_i, summed and passed through a sign function to give one binary output y. It is not a network; it is a threshold logic unit, just like McCulloch-Pitts. The key difference from M-P is what Rosenblatt added: the weights are not programmed by hand — they are adjusted automatically each time the neuron makes a mistake.

**Relationship to Hebbian learning:** Hebb (1949) proposed a biological rule — "neurons that fire together wire together": w_ij increases when neurons i and j are simultaneously active. Rosenblatt was conceptually inspired by this, but his update rule fires on ERROR, not on co-activation. Formally: Δw_i = η·(y − ŷ)·x_i. If the output is correct (y = ŷ), nothing changes. Only a mismatch drives an update. This is error-correction, not Hebbian.

**Distinction from backpropagation (1986):** The perceptron uses a sign (step) activation — non-differentiable, so no gradient can propagate. Backprop requires smooth, differentiable activations (sigmoid, ReLU). The perceptron also has no hidden layers. Modern deep networks are descendants conceptually but not mathematically.

The Mark 1 Perceptron at Cornell learned to recognise letters from photographs. New York Times (1958): "New Navy Device Learns By Doing." It was a physical machine wired with potentiometers as weights.
:::

```{python}
    (2006, "Deep Belief\nNets", "#94a3b8", 10),

    (2017, "Transformer", "#a78bfa", 14),
    (2023, "GPT-4\nLLMs", "#fb923c", 16),
]

fig = go.Figure()

# Winter shading
for x0, x1 in [(1969, 1985), (1995, 2005)]:
    fig.add_shape(type="rect", x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.3, y1=0.7,
                  fillcolor="rgba(248,113,113,0.07)",
                  line=dict(color="rgba(248,113,113,0.2)", width=1, dash="dot"))

    font=dict(size=11, color="#f87171"), showarrow=False)

              line=dict(color="#1e3a5a", width=2))

for year, label, color, size in events:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[year], y=[0.5],
```

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**1969 — First winter**
Minsky & Papert prove perceptron cannot solve XOR.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**1986 — Backpropagation**
Gradients through layers — the key mathematical unlock.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.76em;"}
**2012 — AlexNet** cuts ImageNet error by 10 pp.
Same idea, scaled. Deep learning era begins.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
The Minsky-Papert result was a setback — XOR requires a hidden layer, which the perceptron lacked. The real fix was the sigmoid: a smooth, differentiable activation that lets gradients flow backward through multiple layers. A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere. Backprop was actually derived by Werbos in 1974 but ignored; Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams popularised it in 1986. The second winter was driven by SVMs and kernel methods outperforming neural nets on small datasets. AlexNet won on GPUs — the compute unlock, not a conceptual breakthrough.
:::

## Physics at the core of AI

<div style="position:absolute; top:0.2em; right:0.4em; z-index:10; display:flex; gap:0.7em;">
<figure style="display:flex; flex-direction:row; align-items:center; gap:0.3em; margin:0;">
<figcaption style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">J. Hopfield</figcaption>
<img src="assets/portrait_hopfield.png" style="border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4); height:115px;">
</figure>
<figure style="display:flex; flex-direction:row; align-items:center; gap:0.3em; margin:0;">
<figcaption style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">G. Hinton</figcaption>
<img src="assets/portrait_hinton.png" style="border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.4); height:115px;">
</figure>
</div>

::: {.col-left}

**John Hopfield, 1982** — stores memories as energy minima of the Ising Hamiltonian:

$$E = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{ij} w_{ij} s_i s_j$$

**Geoffrey Hinton** extended this with the Boltzmann distribution $P(s) \propto e^{-E/T}$ — giving neural networks a thermodynamic learning rule.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top:2.5em;"}
**Nobel Prize in Physics 2024**

*"for foundational discoveries enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks"*

— **John J. Hopfield** & **Geoffrey E. Hinton**

Awarded in **Physics**, not Computer Science.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
The Nobel Committee's citation is explicit: Hopfield's use of statistical mechanics to build associative memory, and Hinton's extension to probabilistic models using the Boltzmann distribution, are the foundations.

As accelerator physicists, we think in terms of Hamiltonians, phase spaces, and energy minimisation every day. ML is a natural extension of our toolkit.
:::

## Hopfield networks — neurons as spins

<div class="more-corner"><a class="more-link" href="#/bk-hopfield" title="Backup: Hopfield memory retrieval & capacity"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="m9 9 5 12 1.8-5.2L21 14Z"/><path d="M7.2 2.2 8 5.1"/><path d="m5.1 8-2.9-.8"/><path d="M14 4.1 12 6"/><path d="m6 12-1.9 2"/></svg>click me to know more</a></div>

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.2em;"}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; color:#22d3ee; border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.2em 0.6em; margin-bottom:0.4em;"}
**A collective-effects view:** a beam's coherent modes emerge from *pairwise particle interactions*; a Hopfield memory emerges from *pairwise neuron couplings*. Both are many-body systems governed by an energy function.
:::

The same mathematics describes **Ising spins** and **neural networks**:

::: {style="font-size:0.80em; line-height:1.5;"}
| Ising model | Hopfield network |
|:---|:---|
| Spin $s_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ | Neuron state |
| Coupling $J_{ij}$ | Synaptic weight $w_{ij}$ |
| $E = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum J_{ij}s_is_j$ | Same Hamiltonian |
| Ground state | Stored memory |
:::

:::
::: {.column width="43%"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(7)
N = 10
p = -np.ones((N, N))
p[:, 1] = 1; p[:, 8] = 1       # vertical bars of "H"
p[4:6, 1:9] = 1                 # crossbar

noisy = p.copy()
noisy[np.random.rand(N, N) < 0.28] *= -1

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["Stored memory ξ", "Noisy input (28 % flipped)"],
    horizontal_spacing=0.10)
cscale = [[0, "#f87171"], [0.5, "#0d1b2a"], [1, "#22d3ee"]]
for col, grid in enumerate([p, noisy], 1):
    fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
        z=grid, zmin=-1, zmax=1, colorscale=cscale, showscale=False,
    ), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, showgrid=False, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(showticklabels=False, showgrid=False, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
fig.update_layout(
    height=310, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#0d1b2a",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    margin=dict(l=5, r=5, t=28, b=5),
)
fig
```

::: {style="font-size:0.70em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:center; margin-top:0.15em;"}
Red = −1 (spin ↓) · Cyan = +1 (spin ↑)
:::

::: {style="margin-top:0.5em; font-size:0.72em; border-top:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.2); padding-top:0.4em;"}
**Hebbian learning** — to store pattern $\xi^\mu$:
$$w_{ij} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_\mu \xi_i^\mu \xi_j^\mu$$
:::

:::
::::

::: {.slide-ref}
Hopfield, J.J. (1982). Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities. *PNAS* 79, 2554–2558.
:::

::: notes
**Lead with the collective-effects framing (this is the hook for our audience):** as accelerator physicists we never reason about one particle — we reason about the *collective* behaviour of the whole beam, where coherent modes, instabilities, and space-charge effects emerge from the pairwise interactions between particles, and the whole thing is governed by a Hamiltonian. A Hopfield network is the same kind of object: many simple units (neurons/spins), pairwise couplings, and a global energy whose minima are the interesting states. The difference is only what the minima *mean* — for a magnet, an ordered phase; for the network, a stored memory. So this is not a borrowed metaphor; it is the same many-body bookkeeping we already do for beams, applied to computation.

**The table — Ising model and Hopfield network side by side:**

The Ising model (Lenz 1920, Ising 1925) was invented to describe ferromagnetism. Every iron atom carries a magnetic moment (a spin) that can point up (+1) or down (−1). Neighbouring atoms interact: when both spins are aligned the energy is lower, so the system tends towards alignment. The total energy is E = −½ Σ_{ij} J_{ij} s_i s_j. In equilibrium the system sits at the minimum-energy configuration — all spins aligned (ferromagnet).

Hopfield's 1982 insight: re-read those variables as a neural network:
- Spin s_i ∈ {−1,+1} → neuron i is silent (−1) or active (+1).
- Coupling J_{ij} between atoms i and j → synaptic weight w_{ij} between neurons i and j.
- Energy minimum of the magnet → a stored memory pattern.

This is not an analogy — it is the same equation. A Hopfield network IS a physical spin system. The mathematics of ferromagnetism already contained the mathematics of associative memory; Hopfield made that explicit.

**The Hebbian weight matrix — w_{ij} = (1/N) Σ_μ ξ_i^μ ξ_j^μ:**

To store P patterns ξ^1, ξ^2, ..., ξ^P (each a binary vector of ±1), you set the weight between neurons i and j to the average of their products over all stored patterns. If neurons i and j tend to be in the same state (both +1 or both −1) across many patterns, their weight is large and positive — exactly Hebb's rule. Each pattern contributes one rank-1 outer-product matrix to W; the total weight matrix is their sum (normalised by N).

**The figure — two heatmaps:**
- Left: the letter "H" encoded as a 10×10 grid. Cyan pixels = +1 (spin ↑), red pixels = −1 (spin ↓). This is the stored memory ξ.
- Right: the same pattern with 28% of pixels randomly flipped. This is a corrupted or partial input given to the network at retrieval time. Despite 28% noise, the network converges back to the clean "H". That is content-addressable memory: query with a fragment, retrieve the whole.
:::

---

## Statistical mechanics → deep learning

::: {style="margin-top:0.15em; font-size:0.72em;"}

| Physics concept | ML analogue |
|:---|:---|
| **Hamiltonian / energy** $H(s)$ | **Loss function** $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ |
| **Partition function** $Z = \sum_s e^{-H/T}$ | Normalisation constant (softmax, VAE) |
| **Temperature** $T$ | Learning rate / annealing schedule |
| **Boltzmann distribution** $P \propto e^{-E/T}$ | Softmax output — Boltzmann machine |
| **Phase transition** | Grokking (sharp generalisation threshold) |
| **Langevin dynamics** $\dot{x} = -\nabla E + \eta$ | **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)** |
| **Free energy** $F = -T\ln Z$ | ELBO / variational lower bound (VAE) |

:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.4em; font-size:0.82em;"}
Not metaphors — the **same mathematics**, rediscovered independently.
As accelerator physicists we already speak this language.
:::

::: notes
**Spend ~10 s here — point, don't read.** One sentence: every column is a physics concept the audience already owns, re-labelled for ML — the cleanest being "SGD ≈ Langevin dynamics." Then move on; come back to any row only if asked.

Reference detail for questions: the SGD–Langevin connection was formalised by Welling & Teh (2011). The Boltzmann machine (Ackley, Hinton & Sejnowski 1985) is a literal physical model. Phase transitions in learning (grokking) are an active topic since Power et al. (2022). The deeper Hopfield capacity/retrieval material is now in the backup section if a question goes there.
:::

## Physics metaphors that became real algorithms

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.2em;"}
::: {.column width="52%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; line-height:1.7;"}

- **Simulated annealing** [Kirkpatrick 1983] — slow cooling from metallurgy → global optimisation
- **Renormalisation group** [Mehta & Schwab 2014] — layer-by-layer coarse-graining → deep-net feature hierarchies
- **Langevin dynamics → diffusion models** (2020) — score-based generative models = controlled Brownian motion
- **Double descent & grokking** — phase-transition-like behaviour in model capacity and training time

:::

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {.highlight-box style="font-size:0.74em;"}
**2017–2024 — physics tools enter production**

- Transformers (2017) — attention as a learnable kernel
- Score-based diffusion (2020–22) — Langevin sampling at scale
- AlphaFold2 (2021) — protein fold physics learned, not derived
- GNoME (2023) — 2.2M new crystal structures
- GraphCast (2023) — 10-day weather forecast in 60 s
:::

## 30 years of AI at accelerators

<style>
.ai-milestones table { width: auto !important; margin: 0 auto !important; min-width: 88%; }
.ai-milestones td, .ai-milestones th { padding: 0.45em 1.1em !important; }
</style>

::: {.ai-milestones style="font-size: 0.66em; margin-top: 0.4em;"}

| Year | Facility | Approach | Impact |
|------|----------|----------|--------|
| 1992–94 | Ion source · storage rings | Adaptive NN control (Mead+92); NN orbit correction (Bozoki & Friedman 94) | First ML for accelerator control |
| 2020 | SLAC LCLS | Bayesian optimisation in production | setup hours → ~tens of evaluations |
| 2020 | JLab CEBAF | ML on SRF cavity waveforms | Cavity-fault classification |
| 2024 | DESY / KIT | Cheetah differentiable simulator | 10³–10⁵× faster than tracking codes |
| 2020–23 | CERN · DESY | Reinforcement learning for control & tuning | Autonomous closed-loop control |
| 2024 | KIT KARA | Anomaly detection + energy management | **−30% energy footprint** on real ring |
| 2023–25 | **GANIL SPIRAL2** *(here!)* | DBSCAN RF-fault clustering (LLRF) · SRF cavity heat-load prediction | In-house, transferable across cavities |

:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Edelen et al., *IEEE TNS* 63 (2016) · Duris et al., *PRL* 124 (2020) · Kaiser et al., *PRAB* 27 (2024) · Ghribi et al., *EPN* 56 (2025)
:::

::: notes
30 years from first NNs to production AI systems. The earliest applications are Mead et al. (1992, adaptive NN control of an ion source) and Bozoki & Friedman (1994, NN orbit correction in storage rings) — then two dormant decades limited by compute, before project funding revived the field around 2016 (Edelen+2016). By 2020, BO was in production at LCLS (Duris+2020), with ML-based model-independent stabilisation demonstrated at ALS (Leemann+2019, PRL 123:194801) and differentiable simulation via Cheetah (Kaiser+2024, PRAB). Reinforcement learning entered control with sample-efficient RL at CERN (Kain+2020, PRAB 23:124801) and online RL+BO tuning at DESY (Kaiser+2023). KARA result is not a simulation — measured on the real machine. Last row is home turf: at GANIL/SPIRAL2, unsupervised DBSCAN clustering separates RF-fault signatures on the LLRF system, and a small NN predicts SRF cavity heat-load dissipation sub-watt, ahead of the physical response (credit: C. Lassalle) — the same two families of method (anomaly detection, fast surrogates) you'll meet in Use Cases 1 and 3 today.
:::

These are production results, not simulations. CEBAF (JLab) has run ML-based SRF cavity-fault classification in production since ~2019 (Tennant et al. 2020 is a supervised classifier study; the unsupervised autoencoder in the live-demo notebook is our own illustration, not the CEBAF system). LCLS BO is the Duris+2020 PRL paper — real shots. KARA is the Ghribi+2025 EPN result with measured ring energy reduction. Badger (SLAC) and Geoff are open-source optimisation plugin frameworks that let operators swap algorithms (BO, Nelder-Mead, RL) without rewriting beamline code; both are in active production use at multiple facilities.

This week's 3 challenges sit at exactly these frontiers: **Anomaly Detection** (ESS) in the classification band, **Optimisation** (CLEAR/CLARA) in the mature band, **Surrogate Models** (PALLAS, LWFA) at the least-mature cell in the whole matrix.
:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Snapshot of ML technology maturity in particle accelerators, Jan 2026 [Ghribi+2026-ongoing] — from the AccML living review.
:::

::: notes
Rows are task type (optimisation / classification / modelling), each bar segmented by facility type and ordered left→right by maturity stage (day-to-day operation → social barriers). Read it as: optimisation is the most solved problem across almost every facility type — that's why BO/GP is the classical-ML star of this lecture. Modelling — surrogates and fast simulation — is the least mature column, concentrated at LINAC/light sources and barely emerging at LWFA and future RIs. That is not a coincidence: PALLAS is exactly an LWFA facility, so the Surrogate Models challenge this week is tackling one of the genuinely open frontiers on this map, not a solved problem. Use this to set honest expectations for the harder challenge before the case holders speak.
:::

## {data-auto-animate=true}

<div style="display:flex; gap:0.25em; width:28%; margin-top:0.4em;">
<div data-id="p1" style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.2em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.45); background:rgba(148,163,184,0.06); text-align:center;">
<div style="font-weight:700; font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8;">Raw Data</div>
<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">Waveforms · images<br>logs · set-points</div>
</div>
<div data-id="a1" style="align-self:center; color:#64748b; font-size:0.85em; flex-shrink:0; padding:0 0.05em;">→</div>
<div data-id="p2" style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.2em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.45); background:rgba(148,163,184,0.06); text-align:center;">
<div style="font-weight:700; font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8;">Pre-process</div>
<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">Clean · sync<br>normalise · resample</div>
</div>
</div>

::: {style="display:flex; gap:0.35em; margin:0.4em 0 0.35em 0;"}
::: {.highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**① Clean**
Remove corrupted pulses, stuck sensors, dropouts.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box fragment-index=1 style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**② Synchronise**
Align timestamps across RF, BPM, power supplies.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box fragment-index=2 style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**③ Normalise**
Scale to [−1, 1] — prevents one channel dominating.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box fragment-index=3 style="flex:1; padding:0.35em 0.55em; font-size:0.78em; margin:0;"}
**④ Balance**
SRF faults < 0.1 % of pulses — naïve model learns to ignore them.
:::
:::

::: {style="position:relative;"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(42)
t = np.linspace(0, 4*np.pi, 300)
base = np.sin(t)

# ① Clean — raw with noise + 2 outliers, de-spiked overlay
raw = base + 0.25 * np.random.randn(300)
raw[55] = 3.9
raw[195] = -3.6
cleaned = base + 0.08 * np.random.randn(300)

# ② Synchronise — two channels, one time-lagged
lag = 24
sigA = base
sigB = 0.85 * np.roll(base, lag)

# ③ Normalise — min-max scale cleaned signal to [−1, 1]
mn, mx = cleaned.min(), cleaned.max()
norm = 2.0 * (cleaned - mn) / (mx - mn) - 1.0

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=4,
    subplot_titles=["① Clean", "② Synchronise", "③ Normalise", "④ Balance"],
    horizontal_spacing=0.035,
)

# Panel 1 — Clean
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=raw, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#475569', width=1.0), showlegend=False), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=cleaned, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=1.4), showlegend=False), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[t[55], t[195]], y=[raw[55], raw[195]], mode='markers',
    marker=dict(color='#f87171', size=11, symbol='x',
                line=dict(width=2.2, color='#f87171')), showlegend=False), row=1, col=1)

# Panel 2 — Synchronise
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=sigA, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#60a5fa', width=1.3), showlegend=False), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=sigB, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#a78bfa', width=1.3, dash='dot'), showlegend=False), row=1, col=2)

# Panel 3 — Normalise
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=norm, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=1.4), showlegend=False), row=1, col=3)
fig.add_hline(y=1,  line_dash="dot", line_color="#475569", opacity=0.7, row=1, col=3)
fig.add_hline(y=-1, line_dash="dot", line_color="#475569", opacity=0.7, row=1, col=3)

# Panel 4 — Balance (class imbalance, log scale)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=['normal', 'fault'], y=[99900, 100],
    marker_color=['#334155', '#f87171'],
    text=['99.9 %', '0.1 %'], textposition='outside',
    textfont=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11), showlegend=False), row=1, col=4)

fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=False, showticklabels=False, zeroline=False)
fig.update_yaxes(range=[-1.3, 1.3], row=1, col=3)
fig.update_yaxes(type='log', range=[1.4, 5.9], row=1, col=4)

fig.update_layout(
    height=300, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor='#0d1b2a', plot_bgcolor='#111f30',
    font=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11),
    margin=dict(t=30, b=8, l=8, r=8),
)
fig
```

<div style="position:absolute; left:0; right:0; top:26px; bottom:14px; display:flex; gap:1.1%; pointer-events:none;">
<div class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1" style="flex:1; border-radius:8px; border:2px solid #22d3ee; background:rgba(34,211,238,0.06); box-shadow:0 0 22px rgba(34,211,238,0.5);"></div>
<div class="fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="1" style="flex:1; border-radius:8px; border:2px solid #22d3ee; background:rgba(34,211,238,0.06); box-shadow:0 0 22px rgba(34,211,238,0.5);"></div>
<div class="fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="2" style="flex:1; border-radius:8px; border:2px solid #22d3ee; background:rgba(34,211,238,0.06); box-shadow:0 0 22px rgba(34,211,238,0.5);"></div>
<div class="fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="3" style="flex:1; border-radius:8px; border:2px solid #22d3ee; background:rgba(34,211,238,0.06); box-shadow:0 0 22px rgba(34,211,238,0.5);"></div>
</div>

:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay" data-fragment-index="4">
<div class="callout-box">
A model trained on bad data learns bad behaviour.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">No algorithm compensates for this.</span>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Four preprocessing steps, ordered by how often they are skipped and later regretted. Each press lights up its panel in the strip below. Clean — remove corrupted pulses, stuck sensors, dropouts (panel 1: grey raw with two red outliers, cyan de-spiked result). Synchronise — align timestamps across RF, BPMs, and power supplies, genuinely hard across subsystems with different clocks (panel 2: two channels, one lagged). Normalise to [−1, 1] — so one high-amplitude channel does not dominate the loss (panel 3: scaled between the dotted bounds). Balance — SRF faults are under 0.1% of pulses, so a naïve model reaches 99.9% "accuracy" by always predicting normal and detecting nothing (panel 4: the log-scale class bar makes the imbalance visceral). Punchline on the overlay: a model trained on bad data learns bad behaviour, and no algorithm downstream compensates for that.
:::

<div data-id="p3" style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.2em; border-radius:6px; border:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.45); background:rgba(148,163,184,0.06); text-align:center;">
<div style="font-weight:700; font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8;">Feature extract</div>
<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">FFT · Gaussian fit<br>statistics · domain</div>
</div>
</div>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(7)
n = 256
t = np.linspace(0, 1, n) * 1000  # ms

# Simulated SRF cavity IQ: flat-top pulse with ramps
A = np.zeros(n)
A[30:220] = 1.0
A[30:60]  = np.linspace(0, 1, 30)
A[195:220] = np.linspace(1, 0, 25)
A += 0.03 * np.random.randn(n)

phase_drift = np.zeros(n)
phase_drift[30:220] = np.cumsum(0.003 * np.random.randn(190))
I = A * np.cos(phase_drift)
Q = A * np.sin(phase_drift)

mean_amp   = float(np.mean(A[30:220]))
phase_std  = float(np.std(phase_drift[30:220]) * 180 / np.pi)
fill_frac  = float(np.sum(A > 0.5) / n)

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=[
        "Raw IQ waveform — 256 samples / pulse",
        "Extracted features — 3 scalars",
    ],
    column_widths=[0.62, 0.38],
)

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#60a5fa', width=1.2), name='I'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#a78bfa', width=1.2), name='Q'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=A, mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=2.2), name='|A| amplitude'), row=1, col=1)

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=['Mean<br>amplitude', 'Phase drift<br>(deg)', 'Fill<br>fraction'],
    y=[mean_amp, phase_std, fill_frac],
    marker_color=['#22d3ee', '#f87171', '#fb923c'],
    text=[f'{mean_amp:.3f}', f'{phase_std:.2f}°', f'{fill_frac:.2f}'],
    textposition='outside',
    textfont=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=13),
    showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=2)

fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False,
    title_text="Time (ms)", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False, row=1, col=1)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='#1e3048', zeroline=False,
    range=[0, max(mean_amp, phase_std, fill_frac)*1.4], row=1, col=2)

fig.update_layout(
    height=360, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor='#0d1b2a', plot_bgcolor='#111f30',
    font=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11),
    legend=dict(bgcolor='rgba(0,0,0,0)', font=dict(size=10), x=0.02, y=0.96),
    margin=dict(t=28, b=8, l=10, r=10),
)
fig
```

::: {style="font-size:0.68em; color:#22d3ee; font-weight:600; text-align:center; margin:0.15em 0 0 0;"}
this case: 256 IQ samples → 3 scalars · 99 % compression, fault information retained
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#94a3b8; margin-top:0.3em; line-height:1.55; text-align:center;"}
**The feature map depends on the data** — RF waveform → **FFT peaks · Q · phase drift** &nbsp;·&nbsp; beam image → **Gaussian-fit σ, centroid, image moments** &nbsp;·&nbsp; bunch → **6-D phase-space stats (emittance, Twiss α/β)** &nbsp;·&nbsp; BPM stream → **orbit harmonics**
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="callout-box">
Good features = simpler models + better generalisation.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">Domain knowledge beats brute force.</span>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
The whole point of feature engineering in one figure: for *this* case, 256 raw IQ samples collapse to three physically meaningful scalars — mean amplitude, phase drift, fill fraction — with no loss of the information that distinguishes faults (99% compression). The strip beneath makes the general point: the right feature map depends on the data — FFT peaks/Q/phase for an RF waveform, Gaussian-fit σ and image moments for a screen image, 6-D phase-space statistics (emittance, Twiss) for a bunch, orbit harmonics for a BPM stream. Good features mean smaller models, less data, better generalisation: domain knowledge beats brute force. Then flag the trade-off that sets up UC1: this is the classical route, whereas the autoencoder deliberately skips hand-crafted features and learns its own representation from the raw waveform. Neither is universally right — it depends on how much you trust your physics versus your data.
:::

<div style="font-size:0.46em; color:#475569; margin-top:0.2em; line-height:1.3;">80/20 split<br>cross-val · AUC</div>
</div>
</div>

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:0.72em; color:#cbd5e1; margin:0.05em 0 0.45em 0;"}
**The task decides what "validate" means — and which metric.**
:::

<div style="display:flex; gap:0.4em; margin:0.2em 0 0.4em 0; align-items:stretch;">
<div class="highlight-box" style="flex:1; padding:0.4em 0.6em; font-size:0.66em; margin:0;">
<strong>Anomaly detection</strong> · UC1 <span style="color:#94a3b8;">unsupervised autoencoder</span>
<div style="border-top:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.25); margin:0.3em 0;"></div>
Validate on held-out <strong>normal + unseen fault types</strong>
<div style="margin-top:0.25em; color:#34d399;">✓ ROC-AUC · PR-AUC · F1</div>
<div style="color:#f87171;">✗ accuracy — 99.9 % normal hides everything</div>
</div>
<div class="fragment highlight-box" data-fragment-index="1" style="flex:1; padding:0.4em 0.6em; font-size:0.66em; margin:0;">
<strong>Surrogate regression</strong> · UC3 <span style="color:#94a3b8;">supervised MLP</span>
<div style="border-top:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.25); margin:0.3em 0;"></div>
Validate on inputs <strong>outside the training points</strong>
<div style="margin-top:0.25em; color:#34d399;">✓ R² · RMSE · residual / σ</div>
<div style="color:#f87171;">✗ extrapolation past the training envelope</div>
</div>
<div class="fragment highlight-box" data-fragment-index="2" style="flex:1; padding:0.4em 0.6em; font-size:0.66em; margin:0;">
<strong>Optimisation</strong> · UC2 <span style="color:#94a3b8;">Bayesian optimisation</span>
<div style="border-top:1px solid rgba(148,163,184,0.25); margin:0.3em 0;"></div>
No train/test split — judge <strong>best-so-far vs budget, across seeds</strong>
<div style="margin-top:0.25em; color:#34d399;">✓ regret · convergence · reproducibility</div>
<div style="color:#f87171;">✗ trusting one lucky run</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay" data-fragment-index="3">
<div class="callout-box">
Same word, three protocols.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">Anomaly & surrogate split the data; optimisation measures regret over a budget — there is no test set.</span>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Before any loss curve, fix the most common confusion: "validate" is not one thing. Three task types, three protocols. Anomaly detection (UC1) is unsupervised — you validate the autoencoder on held-out normal data and, critically, on fault types it never saw in training; the metrics are ROC-AUC, precision-recall, F1, never raw accuracy, which is meaningless at 99.9% normal. Surrogate regression (UC3) is supervised — you hold out input points and check R², RMSE, and residuals against the model's own uncertainty; the real failure mode is extrapolation outside the training envelope. Optimisation (UC2) is different in kind — there is no test set at all; you judge a Bayesian-optimisation run by its regret, its convergence against the evaluation budget, and whether it reproduces across random seeds, not by any single lucky run. The takeaway box: same word, three protocols. The next slide drills into the split-and-overfitting story, which applies to the first two.
:::

</div>
</div>

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:0.7em; color:#cbd5e1; margin:0.05em 0 0.4em 0;"}
**Train / validate / test — and the overfitting trap** <span style="color:#64748b; font-size:0.85em;">(supervised tasks)</span>
:::

<div style="display:flex; width:100%; height:2.3em; border-radius:7px; overflow:hidden; font-size:0.6em; font-weight:700; color:#0d1b2a; margin-bottom:0.15em;">
<div style="flex:70; background:#60a5fa; display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;">Train · 70 %</div>
<div style="flex:15; background:#22d3ee; display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;">Val · 15 %</div>
<div style="flex:15; background:#fbbf24; display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;">Test · 15 %</div>
</div>
<div style="display:flex; width:100%; font-size:0.5em; color:#94a3b8; text-align:center; margin-bottom:0.4em;">
<div style="flex:70;">fit the weights</div>
<div style="flex:15;">tune &amp; early-stop</div>
<div style="flex:15;">touch <em>once</em> — unbiased estimate</div>
</div>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

np.random.seed(42)
epochs = np.arange(1, 81)

# Same decay so validation stays ABOVE train at every epoch (never dips below).
decay = 0.72 * np.exp(-epochs / 12)

# Train loss keeps falling — the model fits the TRAINING set ever better
train_loss = decay + 0.020 + 0.005 * np.random.randn(80)

# Validation loss is U-shaped — falls with train, bottoms out, then RISES (overfitting)
val_smooth = decay + 0.050 + 0.0026 * np.clip(epochs - 16, 0, None)
val_loss   = val_smooth + 0.006 * np.random.randn(80)

best     = int(np.argmin(val_smooth)) + 1     # early stop = validation minimum
val_best  = float(val_smooth[best - 1])
test_loss = val_best + 0.013                   # TEST set — one honest evaluation at the best model

fig = go.Figure()
# overfitting region (after the validation minimum)
fig.add_vrect(x0=best, x1=80, fillcolor='rgba(248,113,113,0.06)', line_width=0,
    annotation_text='overfitting', annotation_position='top right',
    annotation_font=dict(color='#f87171', size=10))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=epochs, y=train_loss, name='Train (70 %)',
    line=dict(color='#60a5fa', width=1.8)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=epochs, y=val_loss, name='Validation (15 %)',
    line=dict(color='#22d3ee', width=1.8)))
# best model / early stop at the validation minimum
fig.add_vline(x=best, line_dash='dot', line_color='#fbbf24', opacity=0.85)
fig.add_annotation(x=best, y=0.02, text='best model<br>(early stop)', showarrow=False,
    font=dict(color='#fbbf24', size=9), xanchor='center', yanchor='bottom')
# test set — a single point, evaluated once at the chosen model
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[best], y=[test_loss], mode='markers', name='Test (15 %) — once',
    marker=dict(color='#fbbf24', size=13, symbol='star',
                line=dict(color='#0d1b2a', width=1.2))))

fig.update_layout(
    height=270, autosize=True,
    paper_bgcolor='#0d1b2a', plot_bgcolor='#111f30',
    font=dict(color='#e2e8f0', size=11),
```

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label">⚡&nbsp; Definition — Epoch</div>
<div>
One <strong>epoch</strong> = one complete forward + backward pass over every training sample.<br>
<span style="font-size:0.88em; color:#94a3b8;">
Example: 10 000 pulses, batch 32 → 313 weight updates per epoch.<br>
Training halts when validation loss stops improving — the dashed line marks that minimum (early stopping).
</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="callout-box">
Validate on data the model has never seen — and on faults it has never seen.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">Temporal splits matter more than random splits in accelerator data — and stratify to preserve the &lt; 0.1 % fault rate.</span>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
The three-way split, in order of who touches it: train fits the weights (blue, keeps falling); validation tunes hyper-parameters and triggers early stopping (cyan, U-shaped); test is the amber star — touched exactly once, at the chosen model, for an unbiased estimate (every extra peek leaks it into your choices). The loss curve is the overfitting story: train loss keeps falling while validation loss bottoms out and then turns back up — that widening gap is the model memorising noise, and early stopping freezes it at the validation minimum, where we read the test point. Define "epoch" from the concept box if the audience is mixed. Two accelerator-specific cautions on the last overlay: prefer temporal splits over random ones — random splits leak information between time-correlated neighbouring pulses and flatter the model — and stratify so the sub-0.1% fault rate survives in every split. With only hundreds of labelled faults, 5-fold cross-validation on the training portion is the practical way to get a stable estimate.
:::

::: {.highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.5em; font-size:0.68em; margin:0;"}
**① Latency budget**
Set by the *control loop*, not the model: fast feedback may need sub-ms, daily tuning tolerates seconds.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.5em; font-size:0.68em; margin:0;"}
**② Export &amp; serve**
Deterministic runtime (e.g. ONNX, TorchScript) embeddable in EPICS / TANGO / DOOCS — no Python in the loop.
:::
::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="flex:1; padding:0.3em 0.5em; font-size:0.68em; margin:0;"}
**③ Compress to hardware**
Pruning + quantisation (FP32→INT8) cut latency — at some accuracy cost; trade-off depends on CPU / GPU / FPGA.
:::

**④ Monitor &amp; retrain**
Track output rate and input distributions; retrain when drift crosses a threshold.
:::
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="callout-box">
A model in a notebook is not a deployed model.<br>
<span style="font-weight:400; font-size:0.82em; color:#94a3b8;">Latency, reliability and drift monitoring are engineering problems.</span>
</div>

::: notes
This is where most accelerator-ML projects actually fail. Four constraints, none about the model's accuracy. Latency budget — set by the *control loop*, not the model: a fast feedback loop may demand sub-millisecond inference, while daily tuning tolerates seconds, so match the model to the loop's deadline (don't quote a universal number). Export and serve — convert to a deterministic runtime; ONNX and TorchScript are two examples, embeddable in EPICS / TANGO / DOOCS with no Python interpreter in the loop. Compress to the hardware — pruning and quantisation (e.g. FP32→INT8) cut latency and memory at some accuracy cost, and the right trade-off depends on whether you deploy on CPU, GPU, or FPGA. Monitor and retrain — track output rate and input distributions, retrain when drift crosses a threshold. The log-scale chart is illustrative (the dashed line is an *example* deadline). Closing line: a model in a notebook is not a deployed model — latency, precision, reliability, and drift are engineering problems, not modelling ones.
:::

## The problem: rare faults, no labels

<div class="stepper"><span class="on">① Problem</span> · <span>② Method</span> · <span>③ Results</span> · <span>④ Notebook</span></div>
<div class="more-corner below-stepper"><a class="more-link" href="#/bk-anomaly-landscape" title="Backup: anomaly-detection method landscape"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="m9 9 5 12 1.8-5.2L21 14Z"/><path d="M7.2 2.2 8 5.1"/><path d="m5.1 8-2.9-.8"/><path d="M14 4.1 12 6"/><path d="m6 12-1.9 2"/></svg>click me to know more</a></div>

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.3em; gap:1.5em;"}
::: {.column width="54%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="1"}
Every RF pulse → one **IQ waveform** per cavity at **~1 kHz**.
Machines are **safe by design** — faults are rare.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="2"}
Supervised classifiers need thousands of labelled fault examples per class — **unavailable** in routine operation.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em;" fragment-index="3"}
**Solution:** train on normal pulses only.
Anomaly score = reconstruction error.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="44%"}

<div style="display:grid;">

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.8em 0;" fragment-index="1"}
<span style="font-size:2.2em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee; line-height:1.0;">~1 kHz</span><br>
<span style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; display:block; margin-top:0.4em;">IQ samples per cavity per second<br>1M+ pulses/day in routine operation</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; padding:0.8em 0;" fragment-index="2"}
<div style="font-size:0.68em; font-weight:600; color:#22d3ee; margin-bottom:0.3em;">Four fault classes — superconducting cavity</div>

| Class | Signature |
|---|---|
| **Normal** | Clean trapezoid · Q ≈ 0 |
| **Quench** | Sudden drop mid flat-top |
| **Detuning** | Off-resonance · large Q |
| **Multipacting** | Oscillations on flat-top |

:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.8em 0;" fragment-index="3"}
<span style="font-size:1.8em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee; line-height:1.2;">No fault labels<br>needed</span><br>
<span style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; display:block; margin-top:0.4em;">Anomaly detection trains on normal only</span>
:::

</div>

:::
::::

::: notes
Frame the constraint honestly. Each cavity produces roughly 1 kHz of IQ waveforms — over a million pulses a day — but the machine is safe by design, so genuine faults are vanishingly rare. That kills supervised classification: you cannot collect thousands of labelled examples per fault class in routine operation. The reframe is the key insight: do not try to classify faults, instead model what "normal" looks like and flag anything that deviates. The four fault classes in the table — quench, detuning, multipacting, plus normal — are what we synthesise in the notebook to test the detector. The detector itself never sees them during training; it only ever learns normal.
:::

## What the waveforms look like

<div class="stepper"><span class="on">① Problem</span> · <span>② Method</span> · <span>③ Results</span> · <span>④ Notebook</span></div>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

def _env(t, rise=0.10, fall=0.85):
    return np.piecewise(t.astype(float),
        [t < rise, (t >= rise) & (t <= fall), t > fall],
        [lambda t: t/rise, 1.0, lambda t: (1-t)/(1-fall)])

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)
noise = 0.025

def normal(seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _env(t)
    return env + rng.normal(0, noise, 256), rng.normal(0, noise, 256)

def quench(seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed); qp = rng.integers(80, 160)
    I[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    Q[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    return I, Q

def detuning(seed=2):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _env(t); freq = rng.uniform(3, 7)
    return (env*np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*t)+rng.normal(0,noise,256),
            env*np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*t)+rng.normal(0,noise,256))

def multipacting(seed=3):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed); s, e = 40, 210
    freq = rng.uniform(6, 12); amp = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.22)
    tt = np.linspace(0, 1, e-s)
    I[s:e] += amp*np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    Q[s:e] += amp*np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    return I, Q

cases = [("Normal", normal, "#22d3ee"), ("Quench", quench, "#f87171"),
         ("Detuning", detuning, "#fb923c"), ("Multipacting", multipacting, "#a78bfa")]

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=4,
    subplot_titles=[f"{n} — I" for n,_,_ in cases]+[f"{n} — Q" for n,_,_ in cases],
    vertical_spacing=0.12, horizontal_spacing=0.06)

for col, (name, fn, color) in enumerate(cases, 1):
    I, Q = fn()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        name=name, showlegend=(col==1)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        showlegend=False), row=2, col=col)

fig.update_layout(height=510, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11), margin=dict(l=30, r=10, t=50, b=10),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.08, x=0.5, xanchor="center"))
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig
```

::: notes
Row 1 = I (in-phase), Row 2 = Q (quadrature). Normal: clean trapezoid, Q near zero. Detuning: strong Q. Quench: sharp drop. Multipacting: oscillations.
:::

```{.python}
class RFAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(2, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(64 * 32, latent_dim),  # bottleneck
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(...)    # mirror
```

```{.python code-line-numbers="4-11"}
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(2, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(64 * 32, latent_dim),  # bottleneck
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(...)    # mirror
```
:::

::: notes
**Arrow-driven walk-through.** Each right-arrow press highlights the matching code lines on the left and lights up the corresponding point on the right; earlier points stay visible but dimmed (half-faded), so the list accumulates. The funnel below stays up throughout as the anchor. ① Encoder — two Conv1d stages compress the 2×256 input. ② 1D convolutions slide along the time axis, capturing local structure (rise, drop, oscillations) with far fewer parameters than dense layers. ③ Bottleneck — the whole pulse is squeezed through 16 numbers, so the network can only store a compact model of *normal*; this dimension is the critical hyperparameter (too large and it reconstructs faults too, killing the signal). ④ Decoder mirrors the encoder. Final press: the punchline — anomaly score = reconstruction error, low for normal, high for faults.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

np.random.seed(42)
normal_s = np.random.lognormal(-2.6, 0.4, 200)
fault_s  = np.random.lognormal(-0.7, 0.6, 600)
thresh   = np.percentile(normal_s, 95)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(x=normal_s, xbins=dict(start=0, end=0.55, size=0.009),
    name="Normal", marker_color="#22d3ee", opacity=0.75))
fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(x=fault_s.clip(max=0.55), xbins=dict(start=0, end=0.55, size=0.009),
    name="Faults", marker_color="#f87171", opacity=0.75))
fig.add_vline(x=thresh, line_dash="dash", line_color="#fbbf24", line_width=2.5,
    annotation_text="threshold (95th pct)", annotation_position="top right",
    annotation_font=dict(color="#fbbf24", size=12))
fig.update_layout(barmode="overlay", height=360, autosize=True,
    xaxis_title="Reconstruction error", yaxis_title="Count",
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    legend=dict(bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    margin=dict(l=40, r=10, t=10, b=40))
fig
```

<span style="font-size:1.5em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee; line-height:1.1;">1.000</span><br>
[ROC-AUC — *on synthetic data*]{.metric-label}
:::

:::::
::::::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — ROC-AUC</div>
<div>
A detector needs a threshold — but which one? <strong>ROC-AUC sidesteps the choice.</strong><br>
Sweep <em>every</em> threshold; at each, plot <strong>true-positive rate</strong> (sensitivity) vs <strong>false-positive rate</strong> (1 − specificity). <strong>AUC</strong> = area under that curve.<br>
<strong>0.5</strong> → coin-flip &emsp; <strong>1.0</strong> → perfect separation of normal vs fault.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">Threshold-independent — the right metric when a sub-0.1 % fault rate makes any single fixed cut arbitrary.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Two code ideas to highlight. First, we train only on normal pulses — the y==0 selection — so the network never sees a fault. Second, we set the decision threshold at the 95th percentile of the normal reconstruction errors: a purely unsupervised choice that needs no faults at all. The histogram then shows the payoff — normal errors cluster low, fault errors spread high, with clean separation at the threshold. The headline is ROC-AUC = 1.000, but say "on this synthetic dataset" out loud: real machines are messier and this number will not survive contact with real data — that gap is part of the open-problems discussion later. Use the ROC-AUC concept box for mixed audiences: it is threshold-independent, which is exactly why it is the right metric when no single fixed threshold is meaningful across operating conditions.
:::

## The daily startup problem

<div class="stepper"><span class="on">① Problem</span> · <span>② Method</span> · <span>③ Results</span> · <span>④ Notebook</span></div>
<div class="more-corner below-stepper"><a class="more-link" href="#/bk-opt-landscape" title="Backup: optimisation method landscape"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="m9 9 5 12 1.8-5.2L21 14Z"/><path d="M7.2 2.2 8 5.1"/><path d="m5.1 8-2.9-.8"/><path d="M14 4.1 12 6"/><path d="m6 12-1.9 2"/></svg>click me to know more</a></div>

::: {.col-left}

Every morning on the machine:

1. Run QA checks (output, flatness, energy)
2. Tune magnets until beam is within spec
3. Hand off to the operations team

Currently: **20–45 min of physicist time**, largely manual.

$n$ correctors × $k$ quads → high-dimensional space that grows exponentially for grid search.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**Bayesian Optimisation fits naturally:**

- Works in 2–20 dimensions
- **~50 evaluations** to a good solution
- Model-free — no simulator needed
:::

::: {.key-result .fragment style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Demonstrated in production at SLAC LCLS and across light sources, FELs, and linacs (Duris 2020; Roussel et al. 2024).
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Bayesian prior</div>
<div>
A <strong>prior</strong> P(f) encodes your belief <em>before</em> data — e.g. "the beam response is smooth in magnet space".<br>
Bayes' theorem updates it: <strong>P(f | data) ∝ P(data | f) · P(f)</strong> — the result is the <em>posterior</em>.<br>
BO uses the posterior to pick the next probe: explore where uncertain, exploit where promising.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">Every measurement actively informs the next — no wasted machine evaluations.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Ground the problem in daily operations. Every morning: run QA checks (output, flatness, energy), tune the magnets until the beam is within spec, then hand off to the operations team. Today that is 20–45 minutes of largely manual physicist time. With n correctors and k quadrupoles the search space grows exponentially, so a grid scan is hopeless. BO fits this naturally: it works in 2–20 dimensions, reaches a good solution in tens of evaluations, and is model-free, so it runs directly on the machine with no simulator. Use the Bayesian-prior concept box to give the core idea: encode a belief — "the beam response is smooth in magnet space" — then let Bayes update it with each measurement so every probe is chosen to be maximally informative.
:::

## Cheetah — PyTorch beam dynamics

<div class="stepper"><span>① Problem</span> · <span class="on">② Method</span> · <span>③ Results</span> · <span>④ Notebook</span></div>

<style>
#cheetah-pytorch-beam-dynamics pre { font-size: 0.46em !important; }
</style>

:::::: {.columns}
::::: {.column width="58%"}

:::: {style="display:grid;"}

::: {style="grid-area:1/1;"}
```{.python}
import torch, cheetah

# Beam diverges after a 2 m upstream drift
upstream = cheetah.Segment([cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(2.0))])
beam_in  = upstream.track(cheetah.ParameterBeam.from_twiss(
    energy=torch.tensor(1088.3e6),   # 150 MeV proton, eV
    beta_x=torch.tensor(0.3),
    emittance_x=torch.tensor(1e-6),
    species=cheetah.Species("proton"),
))

# Re-focusing doublet
segment = cheetah.Segment(elements=[
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.1)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.3), name="Q1"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.6)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.3), name="Q2"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.3)),
    cheetah.Screen(name="monitor"),
])

beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1;" fragment-index="1"}

:::

::: notes
Cheetah is the enabling tool: a beam-dynamics code written as a PyTorch module. Two properties matter. It is differentiable — gradients flow straight through the tracking, so it composes natively with machine-learning optimisers — and it runs in milliseconds per call, with the same API whether you point it at a virtual or a real machine. Our setup, which we reuse for the rest of UC2: a 150 MeV proton beam that has diverged after a 2 m drift, re-focused by a two-quad doublet, with the objective being σx + σy at the screen. With the quads switched off, σx + σy is 13.2 mm — that is the untuned baseline BO has to beat, and the convention σx + σy (the sum of both planes) is used consistently across the whole use case.
:::

```{.python}
from skopt import gp_minimize
from skopt.space import Real

NOISE = 0.04  # 4% shot-to-shot noise

def objective(params):
    k1_q1, k1_q2 = params
    segment.Q1.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_q1)
    segment.Q2.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_q2)
    beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
    sigma = (beam_out.sigma_x + beam_out.sigma_y).item()
    if not np.isfinite(sigma): return 0.20
    return sigma * (1 + np.random.normal(0, NOISE))

result = gp_minimize(
    func=objective,
    dimensions=[Real(-15, 15, name="k1_Q1"),
                Real(-15, 15, name="k1_Q2")],
    n_calls=60, n_initial_points=12,
    acq_func="EI",                # Expected Improvement
)
# → ~2.2 mm (8-seed) vs 13.2 mm — a ~6× cut
```
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

n  = 40
ng = 49   # 7×7 grid
iters    = np.arange(1, n + 1)
iters_g  = np.arange(1, ng + 1)

# Explicit representative curves reflecting real notebook results.
# ─── BO: first 8 evals = random LHS init (same policy as random search) ──────
#         evals 9-19: GP model guides → rapid descent to ~2.2 mm
#         evals 20-40: converged (8-seed mean 2.20 ± 0.56 mm)
bo_vals = np.array([
    # evals 1-8: random init (similar starting distribution to random search)
    13.1, 11.8, 12.5, 10.8, 12.2, 10.1, 11.6,  9.4,
    # evals 9-19: GP kicks in, rapid convergence
     7.5,  5.8,  4.4,  3.4,  2.8,  2.5,  2.35, 2.28, 2.24, 2.21, 2.20,
    # evals 20-40: plateau at ~2.2 mm
    2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20,
    2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20, 2.20
])
bo_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(bo_vals)
# UQ band (±1σ across 8 seeds)
bo_std = np.concatenate([np.linspace(2.2, 0.5, 20), np.ones(20) * 0.13])

# ─── Grid 7×7: outer loop k1_Q1, inner loop k1_Q2 ────────────────────────────
#     k1_Q1=-15/-10 rows are strongly defocusing: all values 11–14 mm.
#     Best cell: k1_Q1=-5, k1_Q2=+10 → eval 20 → drops to 2.4 mm.
#     Grid is WORSE than random/BO in early evals (stuck scanning bad rows).
grid_vals = np.array([
    13.5, 12.8, 11.9, 12.5, 13.1, 11.5, 12.7,  # k1_Q1=-15: all bad
    12.3, 11.8, 12.5, 13.0, 11.2, 12.1, 12.8,  # k1_Q1=-10: all bad
    12.9, 12.1, 11.8, 13.2, 11.5,  2.4, 13.4,  # k1_Q1=-5: eval 20 hits!
    13.1, 12.5, 11.9, 12.7, 12.0, 11.3, 12.8,  # k1_Q1=0:  all bad
    12.4, 11.7, 12.9, 13.1, 11.8, 12.5, 11.2,  # k1_Q1=5:  all bad
    12.8, 11.5, 12.3, 11.9,  8.2, 12.0, 13.2,  # k1_Q1=10: one moderate
    12.1, 11.8, 13.0, 12.5, 11.3, 12.7, 11.9   # k1_Q1=15: all bad
])
grid_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(grid_vals)

# ─── Random search: broad decent basin (~3% of space) often found quickly ─────
#     but narrow optimum (~0.4%) almost never reached in 40 evals → ~4.9 mm
rand_vals = np.array([
    # evals 1-8: same random policy as BO (similar starting distribution)
    12.8, 10.9, 13.2, 11.5, 12.0, 10.1, 11.8,  9.5,
    # evals 9-40: hits broad decent basin (3% of space → 66% prob in 40 evals)
    # but never finds the narrow optimum (0.4% → 15% prob)
    12.4, 10.7, 11.5,  9.8, 12.9, 10.3,  5.6, 11.1,
    10.8, 12.2,  9.4, 11.7, 10.5, 12.8,  9.1, 11.3,
    12.1, 10.4,  4.9, 11.8, 10.2,  9.7, 12.5, 10.9,
    11.4,  9.8, 12.1, 10.6, 11.9,  9.3, 12.7, 10.4
])
rand_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(rand_vals)

fig = go.Figure()

# No-quads reference
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=np.ones(n)*13.2, name="No quads",
    line=dict(color="#64748b", width=1.5, dash="dot")))

# Grid
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters_g, y=grid_curve, name="Grid search (7×7)",
    line=dict(color="#94a3b8", width=2, dash="dash")))

# Random
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=rand_curve, name="Random search",
    line=dict(color="#f87171", width=2, dash="dash")))

# BO band (UQ)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=np.concatenate([iters, iters[::-1]]),
    y=np.concatenate([bo_curve+bo_std, (bo_curve-bo_std)[::-1]]),
    fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(34,211,238,0.12)",
    line=dict(color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), showlegend=False))

# BO mean
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=bo_curve, name="Bayesian opt. ± 1σ",
    line=dict(color="#22d3ee", width=3)))

fig.add_annotation(x=39, y=1.5, text="~2.2 mm",
    font=dict(color="#22d3ee", size=13), showarrow=False)

fig.update_layout(height=350, autosize=True,
    xaxis_title="Evaluations", yaxis_title="Best σ_x + σ_y  (mm)",
    yaxis=dict(range=[0.3, 14.5], gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    xaxis=dict(gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    legend=dict(bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", orientation="h",
                y=1.0, x=0.5, xanchor="center", yanchor="bottom"),
    margin=dict(l=40, r=10, t=28, b=40))
fig
```

::: {.notes}
**Reading the convergence plot**

- No-quads baseline (grey dotted): 13.2 mm — the beam without any quadrupoles.
- **Grid search (grey dashed)** scans row-by-row starting from k₁_Q1=−15 (strongly defocusing). All 14 evaluations in the first two rows give 11–14 mm. Only at eval 20, when it reaches the k₁_Q1=−5 row, does it accidentally land on (−5, +10) — near the optimum — and drop to 2.4 mm. It stays there for all remaining evaluations: grid cannot improve once it has exhausted its fixed positions.
- **Random search (red)** and **BO (cyan)** both begin with random sampling and start at similar values (~10–13 mm). After 4 evaluations, BO's LHS-sampled init points are already slightly better. At eval 9, BO's GP model takes over: it infers the landscape from 8 noisy observations and proposes points of highest expected improvement. The curve drops sharply to ~2.2 mm by eval 19.
- Random search keeps sampling uniformly: it hits the **broad decent basin** (~3.6% of the parameter space, σ < 5 mm) around eval 15 by chance, but has only a ~8% probability of finding the **narrow optimum** (0.2% of space, σ < 2 mm) in 40 random evaluations.
- **The 2D verdict is a tie:** averaged over 8 random seeds the final values are statistically indistinguishable — **BO 2.20 ± 0.56 mm vs grid 2.36 ± 0.06 mm** (random 5.17 ± 2.17 mm) — with the 4% measurement-noise floor preventing any method from reaching the 0.80 mm noiseless optimum. BO converges a little faster early on, but its *decisive* advantage is dimensional scaling (below), not the 2D endpoint.
- **Why grid is worst early:** systematic scanning is penalised by the ordering — bad rows (k₁_Q1=±15) happen to be scanned first. Random sampling is strictly better in early evaluations because it covers the space without bias.
- **Dimensionality (measured, not extrapolated):** scaling to a *D*-quad matching section at the *same* 120-evaluation budget, BO reaches **~1.5 mm at D=6** while grid (only 2 points/axis) and random stall near **5 mm** — a controlled experiment in the notebook (§7b), not a hand-waved estimate. A full-resolution 7ᴰ grid would need 7⁶ = 117,649 evaluations; BO needs none. This gentle scaling with dimension is BO's strongest practical advantage on real machines (5–50 parameters).
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Gaussian process vs Bayesian optimisation</div>
<div>
<strong>Gaussian process = the model.</strong> Predicts a <em>mean</em> + <em>variance</em> at every untried setting; the <strong>kernel</strong> sets smoothness (Matérn 5/2 default).<br>
<strong>Bayesian optimisation = the loop.</strong> Fit GP → maximise Expected Improvement (exploit low mean vs explore high variance) → evaluate → repeat.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">GP = the engine ("what does it look like?"); BO = the driver ("where next?").</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

## The speed problem

<div class="stepper"><span class="on">① Problem</span> · <span>② Method</span> · <span>③ Results</span> · <span>④ Notebook</span></div>
<div class="more-corner below-stepper"><a class="more-link" href="#/bk-surrogate-landscape" title="Backup: surrogate-model method landscape"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="m9 9 5 12 1.8-5.2L21 14Z"/><path d="M7.2 2.2 8 5.1"/><path d="m5.1 8-2.9-.8"/><path d="M14 4.1 12 6"/><path d="m6 12-1.9 2"/></svg>click me to know more</a></div>

::: {.col-left style="padding-top: 0.5em;"}

Real-time control needs **millisecond response** — not minutes.

**Workflow:**

1. Run the slow code offline for thousands of inputs
2. Train a neural network on those pairs
3. Call the NN instead of the simulator at runtime

:::

::: {.col-right}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import plotly.graph_objects as go

methods = ["TraceWin<br>(1 call)", "G4beamline<br>(1 call)",
           "Cheetah<br>(1 000 calls)", "Surrogate<br>(1 000 calls)"]
times = [60_000, 600_000, 770, 1.2]
colors = ["#64748b", "#475569", "#f87171", "#22d3ee"]
labels = ["1 min", "10 min", "770 ms", "1.2 ms"]

fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
    x=methods, y=times, marker_color=colors,
    text=labels, textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(color=colors, size=14),
))
fig.update_layout(
    yaxis=dict(type="log", gridcolor="#1e3048",
               tickvals=[1, 1e3, 1e5, 1e6],
               ticktext=["1 ms", "1 s", "1 min", "10 min"]),
    xaxis=dict(gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    height=460, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=12),
    margin=dict(t=50, b=10, l=50, r=10), showlegend=False,
)
fig
```

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Typical speedup: **10³–10⁵×** · error **< 1%** in domain
:::

::: notes
The motivation in one chart, on a log scale: TraceWin and G4beamline take minutes per call, Cheetah takes milliseconds, and a trained surrogate takes microseconds. The workflow is the standard recipe — run the slow code offline for thousands of inputs, fit a network to the input-output pairs, then call the network instead of the simulator at runtime. Typical speedups are 10³ to 10⁵× with under 1% error. Stress "in domain": a surrogate interpolates beautifully inside the region it was trained on and extrapolates badly outside it, so the training distribution defines where you are allowed to trust it.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(0)
n = 500
sigma_true = (np.random.gamma(2.0, 5.0, n) + 0.5).clip(0.5, 30)
sigma_pred = sigma_true + np.random.normal(0, 0.002*sigma_true+0.001, n)

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["σ_x — Surrogate vs. Cheetah", "σ_y — Surrogate vs. Cheetah"])

for col in [1, 2]:
    lo, hi = sigma_true.min(), sigma_true.max()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=sigma_true, y=sigma_pred, mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color="#22d3ee", size=3, opacity=0.5),
        showlegend=False), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[lo,hi], y=[lo,hi], mode="lines",
        line=dict(color="#f87171", dash="dash", width=1.5),
        showlegend=False), row=1, col=col)

fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Cheetah (mm)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Surrogate (mm)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048")
fig.update_layout(height=380, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11), margin=dict(l=40,r=10,t=35,b=25))
fig
```

<div style="display:flex; gap:1.8em; justify-content:center; margin-top:0.5em;">
<div style="text-align:center;"><span style="font-size:0.85em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee;">1.0000</span><br><span style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8;">R²</span></div>
<div style="text-align:center;"><span style="font-size:0.85em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee;">0.001 mm</span><br><span style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8;">MAE</span></div>
<div style="text-align:center;"><span style="font-size:0.85em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee;">~600×</span><br><span style="font-size:0.55em; color:#94a3b8;">speedup</span></div>
</div>

:::::
::::::

::: notes
Concrete numbers. A tiny MLP — 2 → 128 → 128 → 128 → 2 with Tanh activations — maps the two quad strengths to (σx, σy). Training uses 5000 Cheetah calls offline, about 3 seconds of data generation, then 300 epochs. The parity plot sits right on the diagonal: R² ≈ 1.00, MAE around 0.001 mm, roughly 600× speedup. Two honesty caveats straight from the notebook. The ~600× is deliberately qualitative — run-to-run timing varies by a few hundred-fold depending on hardware and batching, so do not quote a precise figure. And the learned input-output sensitivity is near-uniform — each quad affects both transverse planes — not the clean diagonal one might naively expect, because every quadrupole focuses in one plane and defocuses in the other.
:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay" data-fragment-index="6">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Explainability (XAI)</div>
<div>
<strong>SHAP</strong>: assigns each input a numerical contribution to the prediction (Shapley values from game theory, 1953 — model-agnostic).<br>
<strong>LIME</strong>: fits a local linear model around one specific prediction to explain it locally.<br>
High-consequence control loops (medical devices, safety systems) increasingly require auditable, explainable decisions under emerging AI regulation (e.g. the EU AI Act's high-risk tier) — a bar general accelerator control will likely be held to as well.<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">In practice: SHAP tells you whether the model learned beam physics or a spurious data artefact.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Five honest open problems, each framed as an accelerator question rather than an abstract ML one. Explainability — before an operator hands control authority to a model, the decision has to be auditable; regulation for high-consequence control loops (the EU AI Act's high-risk tier for medical devices is the sharpest existing example) is one preview of where this is heading. Cross-facility transfer — a model trained at Centre A rarely works at Centre B without re-tuning. Agnostic integration — getting one model into EPICS, TANGO, or DOOCS through a vendor-neutral adapter layer (latency target depends on the use case — keep it general here). Data and model standards — there is still no shared schema and no FAIR ML models across facilities. And agentic orchestration — LLM planners coordinating specialist ML tools, an emerging architecture. The balance to strike: these are genuinely active research, but the lecture has just shown AI delivering value today. Use the XAI concept box for SHAP versus LIME — and the punchline that SHAP tells you whether the model learned beam physics or a spurious artefact in your data.
:::

::: {.fragment .highlight-box style="font-size:0.60em; margin-top:0.5em; line-height:1.7;"}
**Foundation models** pretrain on multi-facility data &nbsp;·&nbsp; **RL** closes the loop on the real machine (CERN, DESY) &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Generative models** synthesise rare fault data &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Digital twins** = surrogate + live sensors, enabled by the ~600× speedup (→ TwinRISE)
:::

::: notes
This is an appetizer, not a full menu. Foundation models (e.g. CERN's accelerator-specific LLM prototypes), PINNs (several groups at SNS and ESS), and RL (Kain+2020, Hirlaender+2020) are all active research directions with published results. Digital twins are the natural endpoint of the surrogate use case: a surrogate plus live sensor feeds plus continuous updating, tracking the actual machine rather than a static design model — and it is the ~600× surrogate speedup that makes a real-time twin feasible at all. TwinRISE (Horizon Europe 2026–2030, 19 institutions, federated for data sovereignty) is the European vehicle; more on it in the opportunities slide. The key message: the gap between today's lecture and the frontier is smaller than students often assume. Bubble position is schematic — readiness is illustrative, not a formal TRL score.
:::

## Summary

::: {style="font-size:0.82em; color:#cbd5e1; margin:0.4em 0 0.8em;"}
**AI is broader than deep learning.** We built three methods end to end — two neural, one classical (BO/GP) — on real beam-physics problems: **problem → method → result → runnable notebook.**
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.84em; line-height:1.75;"}
- **Three use cases, end to end** — fault detection (AUC ≈ 1) · beam tuning (BO + Cheetah, advantage grows with dimension) · surrogate (R² ≈ 1, ~600× faster).
- **Physics ↔ AI** — Hopfield, Boltzmann machines, the 2024 Nobel in Physics: we are natural practitioners, not outsiders.
- **The model is rarely the bottleneck** — data quality, features and the pipeline decide whether it works.
- **Deployment ≠ accuracy** — latency, drift, explainability and integration are the real blockers to production.
:::

## Hopfield — memory retrieval and capacity {#bk-hopfield}

:::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.3em; gap:1.5em;"}
::: {.column width="54%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="1"}
**① Ball in a valley** — memories are energy minima.
Noisy input rolls downhill → arrives at nearest stored pattern.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em; margin-bottom:0.5em;" fragment-index="2"}
**② Spin update** — $s_i \leftarrow \text{sign}(\sum_j w_{ij} s_j)$
Energy decreases at every step: **guaranteed convergence**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out style="border-left:3px solid rgba(34,211,238,0.5); padding:0.35em 0.7em; font-size:0.76em;" fragment-index="3"}
**③ Capacity ≈ 0.14 N** — beyond this, retrieval fails **catastrophically** (sharp phase transition, not gradual).
:::

:::
::: {.column width="44%"}

<div style="display:grid;">

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1;" fragment-index="1"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import plotly.graph_objects as go

x = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 90)

X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

E = (
    - 2.2 * np.exp(-2.2*((X - 1.3)**2 + (Y - 1.1)**2))
    - 2.2 * np.exp(-2.2*((X + 1.3)**2 + (Y + 1.1)**2))
    + 0.28*(X**2 + Y**2)
)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Contour(
    z=E, x=x, y=y,
```
