```{python}
    contours=dict(showlabels=False, coloring='fill'),
    showscale=False, ncontours=22, opacity=0.9,
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[1.3, -1.3], y=[1.1, -1.1], mode="markers+text",
    marker=dict(color="#fbbf24", size=14, symbol="star"),
    text=["Memory 1", "Memory 2"],
    textposition=["top right", "bottom left"],

tx = [0.35, 0.60, 0.88, 1.10, 1.25, 1.30]

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=tx, y=ty, mode="lines+markers",

fig.add_annotation(x=0.35, y=0.05, text="Noisy / partial input",

fig.add_annotation(x=0.88, y=0.62, text="each update:<br>energy ↓",

fig.add_annotation(x=1.3, y=1.1, text="recalled<br>memory",
    font=dict(size=9, color="#fbbf24"),
    showarrow=True, ax=38, ay=-28,
    arrowcolor="#fbbf24", arrowwidth=1.5)
fig.add_annotation(x=-1.3, y=-1.1, text="energy<br>minimum",

fig.update_layout(
    height=270, autosize=True,

    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"),

```

:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.5em 0.5em;" fragment-index="2"}
<div style="font-size:1.1em; color:#22d3ee; font-weight:700; margin-bottom:0.5em; font-family:monospace;">
s<sub>i</sub> ← sign(Σ w<sub>ij</sub> s<sub>j</sub>)
</div>
<div style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; line-height:1.6;">
Hebb rule · ΔE ≤ 0 per step<br>
<span style="color:#fbbf24;">Same physics as spin relaxation</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible style="grid-area:1/1; text-align:center; padding:1.8em 0;" fragment-index="3"}
<span style="font-size:2.4em; font-weight:800; color:#22d3ee; line-height:1.0;">0.14 N</span><br>
<span style="font-size:0.72em; color:#94a3b8; display:block; margin-top:0.4em;">Capacity limit · recall error: 0 → 50%</span>
:::

</div>

:::
::::

::: {.slide-ref}
Amit, Gutfreund & Sompolinsky (1985). Storing infinite numbers of patterns in a spin-glass model. *PRL* 55, 1530.
:::

::: notes
**① The contour plot — energy landscape:** the axes are abstract coordinates in the space of all possible network states; each point is one configuration of all N neurons. Colour = energy. The two yellow stars are stored memories (energy minima); the orange trajectory is a noisy input rolling downhill to the nearest one. Particle-in-a-potential dynamics, where the "particle" is the whole network state.

**② Spin update s_i ← sign(Σ_j w_{ij} s_j):** one can prove ΔE ≤ 0 at every update (E = −½ Σ w_{ij} s_i s_j, w symmetric), so convergence to a local minimum is guaranteed — identical to spin relaxation in an Ising magnet at zero temperature.

**③ Why 0.14N:** with load α = P/N, the other P−1 patterns inject cross-talk noise ~√(P/N). Amit–Gutfreund–Sompolinsky (1985) computed the critical α_c ≈ 0.138 with the replica method (spin-glass theory) — a genuine field-theoretic result, not a scaling estimate. The transition is first-order: below it recall error ≈ 0, at it the error jumps to ~0.5. A 1000-neuron network stores ~138 patterns, then breaks catastrophically.
:::

## How Minsky & Papert froze the field (1969) {.smaller #bk-minsky}

::: {.col-left}

**1969 — *Perceptrons*** (Minsky & Papert) proved a single-layer perceptron **cannot compute XOR**, nor any non-linearly-separable function.

Impact as much *sociological* as mathematical:

- US funding agencies read it as "neural nets are a dead end"
- Connectionist funding collapsed through the 1970s
- The field pivoted to **symbolic AI** / expert systems
- Revived only by **backprop** (Werbos 1974; Rumelhart–Hinton–Williams 1986) — which trains the hidden layers they dismissed

:::
::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**The irony**

XOR *is* solvable — with **one hidden layer**. The authors knew it, but wrongly argued such nets could never be trained at scale. Backprop proved them wrong 17 years later.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.6em;"}
One influential "impossibility" result can freeze a direction for a decade. Scepticism cuts both ways.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Minsky & Papert (1969). *Perceptrons*, MIT Press. · Werbos (1974) · Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986), *Nature* 323, 533.
:::

::: notes
Backup for the AI-winters slide. The take-home is the sociology of science, not just the XOR maths: a single authoritative result, amplified by funding decisions, set the field back a decade even though the technical fix (hidden layers) was already conceivable. Good answer if someone asks "why did it take so long?"
:::

---

## Backup — Bayesian optimisation internals {.smaller #bk-bo-internals}

::: {.col-left}

**Expected Improvement** acquisition function:

$$\alpha_{\text{EI}}(x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\max(0,\; f_{\text{best}} - f(x))\big]$$

For a GP posterior with mean $\mu(x)$, std $\sigma(x)$, and $z = \dfrac{f_{\text{best}} - \mu(x)}{\sigma(x)}$:

$$\alpha_{\text{EI}}(x) = \sigma(x)\,\big[\,z\,\Phi(z) + \phi(z)\,\big]$$

- $\Phi, \phi$ — standard-normal CDF / PDF
- term 1 **exploits** (low predicted mean), term 2 **explores** (high variance)
- next probe = $\arg\max_x \alpha_{\text{EI}}(x)$

:::
::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box style="font-size:0.82em;"}
**The kernel is the prior on smoothness**

- **Matérn 5/2** — twice-differentiable; default for physical systems
- **RBF** — infinitely smooth (often *too* smooth for real data)
- **Periodic** — cyclic signals (RF phase)
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.6em; font-size:0.82em;"}
Kernel choice encodes physics — the single most consequential modelling decision in BO.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Backup for UC2. If asked "how does BO actually pick the next point": EI balances exploit (first term) and explore (second term) in closed form from the GP posterior. The kernel question is the one experts ask — Matérn 5/2 is the sane default because real beam responses are continuous but not infinitely smooth; RBF over-smooths and can miss sharp features.
:::

---

## Backup — BO vs grid / random as dimension grows

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.2em;"}
Controlled experiment (notebook 02 §7b): a *D*-quad matching section, **the same budget B = 120 evaluations** for every method, log(σ_x+σ_y) objective, 4% noise, 3 seeds.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.92em;"}
| Dimension | Grid | Random | **Bayesian opt.** |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **D = 2** (2 quads) | 5.1 mm | 4.7 mm | **3.4 mm** |
| **D = 4** (4 quads) | 7.2 mm | 3.0 mm | **1.2 mm** |
| **D = 6** (6 quads) | 5.9 mm | 4.6 mm | **1.5 mm** |
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.5em; font-size:0.84em;"}
At D = 6, BO is ~3× better than either baseline and **every seed wins**. A full-resolution 7ᴰ grid would need 7⁶ = **117,649** evaluations; BO used 120.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.74em; color:#94a3b8; margin-top:0.4em; line-height:1.5;"}
Why grid/random collapse: usable volume shrinks as ~rᴰ, so a fixed budget covers exponentially less of the space. BO builds a surrogate and spends evaluations where they matter. And note D = 4/6 reach a *smaller* spot than D = 2 — more quads give more focusing freedom, which BO exploits and classical methods cannot.
:::

::: notes
This is the slide that backs the "BO wins as dimension grows" claim with measured numbers, not extrapolation. The 2D result is honestly a near-tie; the story only becomes decisive at D = 4 and beyond. Pull this up if anyone challenges why BO over a simple grid.
:::

---

## Backup — why an autoencoder, not a classifier? {#bk-ae-classifier}

::: {style="font-size:0.82em;"}
| Approach | Needs fault labels? | Detects *unseen* fault types? | Fit for label-scarce RF |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|
| **Threshold / interlock** | no | no — only hard-coded limits | safety net, not detection |
| **Supervised classifier** (Tennant 2020) | **yes — many per class** | no | great *when* labels exist |
| **Autoencoder (ours)** | **no — normal data only** | **yes** | fits label-scarce ops |
:::

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top:0.5em; font-size:0.84em;"}
The autoencoder learns "normal"; anything it reconstructs poorly is flagged — including fault modes never seen in training. A supervised classifier can only recognise the classes it was trained on.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.5em; font-size:0.82em;"}
Trade-off: the autoencoder tells you *something is wrong*, not *what*. Pair it with a classifier once labels accumulate.
:::

::: notes
Backup for UC1, and the honest framing of the Tennant-2020 comparison: the CEBAF system is a supervised classifier on labelled data — the right tool there. Our autoencoder is the right tool when no labels exist, which is the common reality in routine operation. They are complementary, not competing.
:::

---

## Backup — uncertainty quantification, in numbers {#bk-uq}

::: {.col-left}

Two ways to make the MLP surrogate report confidence (notebook 03):

**Deep ensemble** — train N models from different initialisations; the spread of their predictions is the uncertainty.

**MC-dropout** — keep dropout active at inference and run K stochastic forward passes.

:::
::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box style="font-size:0.84em;"}
**Measured — MC-dropout, σ_x+σ_y**

- R² ≈ 0.999
- σ_MC ≈ 0.13 mm
- ~99.7% empirical coverage (within ±3σ)
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.5em; font-size:0.82em;"}
**Epistemic** (reducible by more data) vs **aleatoric** (irreducible noise). For control you want *calibrated* σ — the error bars should match the actual errors.
:::

::: notes
Backup for UC3. The key word is "calibrated": a model that reports σ = 0.13 mm but is routinely wrong by 1 mm is worse than useless in a control loop. Coverage near the nominal 99.7% (±3σ) is the check that the uncertainty is honest.
:::

---

## Backup — reinforcement learning in the control loop {#bk-rl}

::: {.col-left}

**Setup:** the agent observes machine state $s$ (BPMs, losses), takes action $a$ (corrector / quad set-points), receives reward $r$ (e.g. −beam loss), and learns a policy $\pi(a\,|\,s)$ that maximises cumulative reward.

**Why RL, not BO, here?** RL *amortises*: it learns a reusable policy for a recurring sequential task, where BO re-optimises from scratch every time.

:::
::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box style="font-size:0.82em;"}
**Demonstrated**

- **CERN** — sample-efficient RL for steering (Kain et al. 2020)
- **DESY** — online RL + BO injector tuning (Kaiser et al. 2023)
- **RL4AA** — community challenge & open benchmarks
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top:0.6em; font-size:0.8em;"}
Open problem: sample efficiency and *safe* exploration on a live machine.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.slide-ref}
Kain et al., *PRAB* 23, 124801 (2020) · Hirländer et al. (2020) · Kaiser et al. (2023)
:::

::: notes
Backup for the futures slide, since RL is named but never shown. The crisp distinction to offer: BO is single-shot optimisation, RL learns a policy for a repeated sequential task. The blocker is not capability but safe exploration — you cannot let an agent try arbitrary set-points on a live beam without bounding the risk.
:::

## Backup — anomaly detection: method landscape {#bk-anomaly-landscape}

```{python}

#| eval: true

# x: training data volume needed (0=minimal → 2=large dataset)
# y: suitability for rare-event / SRF fault detection (1=poor → 5=excellent)

    ("Threshold rules",  0.00, 1.1, 20, "#475569", "bottom right"),
    ("PCA anomaly",      0.30, 2.0, 22, "#64748b", "top right"),

               showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False),
    margin=dict(l=90, r=30, t=20, b=70),
)
fig
```

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.3em; font-size: 0.78em;"}
**This lecture:** Autoencoder — unsupervised, normal-data only, scales to 1 kHz waveform streams.
:::

::: notes
The same decision map as before, zoomed into anomaly detection. x is the training data required, y is suitability for rare-event detection. The autoencoder (cyan star) sits in the sweet spot: it trains on normal data only, needs no fault labels, and scales to kHz waveform streams. The classical methods on the left — threshold rules, PCA, isolation forest — are cheaper but weaker on high-dimensional waveforms. The VAE and LSTM-autoencoder top-right are more powerful but more data-hungry and harder to deploy. We pick the autoencoder as the best balance for a label-scarce facility.
:::

## Backup — optimisation: method landscape {#bk-opt-landscape}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

# x: log10(typical evaluations to converge) — lower = better
# y: works on real machine without gradient (1=no → 5=yes)
# Scope: static beam-tuning optimisation (not sequential online control)
methods = [
    ("Grid Search",          4.3, 4.6, 22, "#475569", "top left"),
    ("MOGA / GA",            3.6, 4.8, 24, "#a78bfa", "top right"),
    ("RL † online ctrl",     3.8, 5.0, 22, "#a78bfa", "bottom right"),
    ("Random Search",        2.5, 4.5, 24, "#94a3b8", "bottom right"),
    ("CMA-ES",               2.7, 4.7, 22, "#64748b", "top right"),
    ("Nelder-Mead",          2.3, 3.7, 22, "#94a3b8", "bottom left"),
    ("Gradient descent",     1.8, 1.4, 24, "#fb923c", "bottom right"),
    ("Bayesian Opt. ★",     1.6, 5.0, 42, "#22d3ee", "top right"),
]

fig = go.Figure()
for name, logx, y, size, color, pos in methods:
    is_pick = "★" in name
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[logx], y=[y], mode="markers+text",
        marker=dict(size=size, color=color,
            line=dict(color="#e2e8f0" if is_pick else "#0d1b2a",
                      width=2.5 if is_pick else 1.5)),
        text=[f"<b>{name}</b>" if is_pick else name],
        textposition=pos,
        textfont=dict(size=12 if is_pick else 10, color=color),
        showlegend=False,
    ))

fig.add_annotation(x=1.6, y=4.35, text="← best quadrant",
    showarrow=False, font=dict(size=10, color="#fbbf24"), xanchor="left")
fig.add_annotation(x=4.95, y=0.85,
    text="† RL: best for sequential online control, not single-shot optimisation",
    showarrow=False, font=dict(size=9, color="#64748b"), xanchor="right")

fig.update_layout(
    height=530, autosize=True, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    xaxis=dict(title="Evaluations to converge  (← fewer = better)",
               range=[1.0, 5.0],
               tickvals=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
               ticktext=["10", "100", "1 000", "10 000", "100 000"],
               showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False,
               autorange="reversed"),
    yaxis=dict(title="Real machine compatible (no gradient required)",
               range=[0.8, 5.5],
               tickvals=[1, 3, 5],
               ticktext=["No<br>(needs gradient)", "Partial", "Yes<br>(model-free)"],
               showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False),
    margin=dict(l=110, r=30, t=20, b=80),
)
fig
```

::: {.slide-ref}
Duris et al., *PRL* 124 (2020) · Roussel et al., *PRAB* 27 (2024) · Emma et al., *Nat. Mach. Int.* 1 (2019) · Kain et al., *Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams* 23 (2020)
:::

::: notes
Decision map for optimisation. x is evaluations to converge — fewer is better, and the axis is reversed so "good" is to the right — and y is whether the method works on a real machine without gradients. Bayesian optimisation (cyan star) is in the best quadrant: gradient-free and sample-efficient, converging in tens of evaluations. Two things to point out. The footnote on RL: it is excellent for sequential online control but not single-shot tuning, so it is not really a competitor for this specific task. And gradient descent sits at the bottom because you rarely have usable gradients on a real machine — which is exactly the gap Cheetah closes on the next slide.
:::

:::

<div class="fragment slide-callout-overlay">
<div class="concept-callout-box">
<div class="concept-callout-label"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#fbbf24" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="flex-shrink:0;vertical-align:-0.15em;"><path d="M15 14c.2-1 .7-1.7 1.5-2.5 1-.9 1.5-2.2 1.5-3.5A6 6 0 0 0 6 8c0 1 .2 2.2 1.5 3.5.7.7 1.3 1.5 1.5 2.5"/><path d="M9 18h6"/><path d="M10 22h4"/></svg> Concept — Uncertainty quantification</div>
<div>
<strong>Epistemic</strong> (model) uncertainty: caused by insufficient data — <em>reducible</em> by collecting more samples.<br>
<strong>Aleatoric</strong> (data) uncertainty: inherent measurement noise — <em>irreducible</em>.<br>
Methods: <strong>deep ensembles</strong> (spread of N models) · <strong>MC Dropout</strong> (stochastic inference) · <strong>Gaussian processes</strong> (closed-form variance).<br>
<span style="color:#94a3b8; font-size:0.92em;">Knowing <em>when the model is uncertain</em> is as important as the prediction itself — especially for safety-critical beam control.</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Decision map for surrogates. x is the training samples needed, y is the quality of uncertainty quantification. The MLP (cyan star) is fast and reasonably data-efficient but gives no uncertainty estimate on its own — which is exactly why the notebook adds deep ensembles and MC-dropout on top of it. Gaussian processes have excellent, closed-form, calibrated uncertainty but scale badly to large datasets; ensemble MLPs buy you uncertainty at N times the cost. Use the UQ concept box to draw the key distinction: epistemic uncertainty is model uncertainty from too little data and is reducible by collecting more; aleatoric uncertainty is inherent measurement noise and is irreducible. For safety-critical beam control, knowing when the model does not know is as important as the prediction itself.
:::
